..
KEY MESSAGE 1...Showers and thunderstorms return and increase 
along with increasingly more humid for the first half of the 
week. There is potential for strong to severe thunderstorms both
Monday and Tuesday, and potential for areas of heavy rain 
leading to flash flooding on Tuesday.

As a strong upper-level ridge expands into the Plains early 
next week, northwesterly flow aloft will occur across much of 
the East. This ridge gets pushed back some as a potentially 
strong upper-level trough in eastern Canada sends spokes of 
energy southeastward across the Great Lakes and Northeast. This 
will initially allow for the upper-level trough to become more 
carved out across the Northeast by later this weekend. Some 
guidance maintains a vigorous shortwave riding over the ridge 
and sliding southeastward across the Great Lakes Monday and then
across the Northeast during Tuesday. This results in some model
solutions continuing to close off the trough across the 
Northeast Tuesday into Wednesday. Some other guidance is slower 
and weaker and thus does not close it off or briefly closes it 
off a day or two later. The upper-level system will drive 
surface low pressure and a cold front our way Tuesday into 
Wednesday. It will become much more humid during the first half 
of next week, with dew points looking to surge on Tuesday.

This will all result in an increase in convective chances 
Monday and especially Tuesday into Wednesday. While there 
remains some differences among the model guidance on the timing 
and strength of the features diving southeastward early next 
week, the setup would continue to favor upstream convective 
development given northwesterly flow aloft.

Monday's setup looks to be a pulsy, single to multi cell 
cluster environment with low shear and modest instability. Deep 
layer shear will be weak, only around 10-20 kts. Instability 
looks to be in the 1000-2000 J/kg range. DCAPE is also modest 
around 500-1000 J/kg. This setup will favor scattered, hit or 
miss type showers and thunderstorms developing during the 
afternoon hours, with a marginal risk of severe thunderstorms. 
Any stronger storms could produce isolated strong to marginally 
severe wind gusts and brief heavy downpours. Our entire area is 
outlooked in a MARGINAL Risk (level 1 out of 5) for severe 
thunderstorms on Monday. Scattered showers and storms may 
continue overnight as better forcing arrives aloft, though the 
severe threat will likely be minimal overnight.

Tuesday looks to feature the most widespread showers and
thunderstorms. Height falls and jet dynamics aloft will favor
convective development nearly all day as surface low pressure 
develops just to our west. This will keep a steady stream of 
warm, moist air pumping into the area and keeping the 
environment conditionally unstable despite cloud cover. PWats 
will rise to near 2" by the end of the day. Some models suggest
we could have a stalled or slow moving frontal boundary across
the central or northern portion of the forecast area, which
could act as a focusing mechanism for heavy rainfall. Heavy 
rain leading to flash flooding could end up being a bigger 
concern and greater impact than the severe thunderstorm threat.

Long story short, a very active day is expected convection 
wise on Tuesday. A due southerly surface flow and the dynamics 
aloft will favor areas along and northwest of the I-95 corridor
and/or the frontal boundary to be the focus of the heaviest 
rain, and areas along and southeast of the I-95 corridor and/or
the frontal boundary where convection is less messy and the 
environment a bit less contaminated being the greater severe 
thunderstorm threat depending on exactly how the convection 
evolves. That still remains a little unclear at the moment, and 
may depend on how storms evolve upstream Monday and Monday 
night.

WPC has outlooked much of our area from the I-95 corridor and 
north in a SLIGHT Risk (level 2 out of 4) for excessive rainfall
for Tuesday. SPC has outlooked the southern half of our area 
from the Philly metro and south in a SLIGHT Risk (level 2 out of
5) for severe thunderstorms on Tuesday.

On Wednesday, low pressure looks to be offshore to our east. 
Scattered showers and storms will likely develop again by 
afternoon, at least across our NJ and PA zones, but the severe 
thunderstorm and heavy rain threat look to be lower and focused
across southern New England given the setup. We'll continue to
monitor this period though.

Thursday and Friday will feature continued chances of scattered
showers and storms (20-40% chance), especially Thursday as the
Tuesday-Wednesday system slowly pushes east. Details on the late
week period are very uncertain.
